The developing eggs of the Kanadi kingfish (Scomberomorus plurilineatus) provide a remarkably small starting point for this large, fast-growing scombrid. At the moment of hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerging from the pelagic egg possesses a wet weight at birth of just 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams], a value derived from the standard 0.5 mm egg diameter observed in the congeneric narrow-barred Spanish mackerel (Scomberomorus commerson). This minuscule mass, characteristic of pelagic spawners that produce vast numbers of small eggs, represents the entire endogenous energy reserve from which the lecithotrophic larva must draw before initiating first exogenous feeding. The species exhibits a truly impressive growth trajectory from this modest beginning, ultimately reaching an ultimate wet weight of 12,500 grams [Wwi = 12,500 grams] as a fully grown spawning adult. Such an immense gain, spanning nearly eight orders of magnitude in body mass, underscores a life-history strategy centered on rapid juvenile growth and high fecundity, a pattern common among epipelagic piscivores of the tropical Indo-West Pacific.

Field surveys and growth reconstructions from otolith increment analyses have allowed researchers to establish several key size benchmarks in the ontogeny of Scomberomorus plurilineatus. The most comprehensive studies indicate that an individual attains sexual maturation upon reaching a fork length at puberty of 80 centimeters [Lp = 80 centimeters]. This morphological threshold, recorded from the anterior snout to the fork of the caudal fin, corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3,700 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,700 grams], calculated from the allometric relationship between length and mass. This weight is reached well before the species achieves its theoretical maximum size, which is defined by an ultimate fork length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters]. The gap between the size at puberty and the ultimate fork length implies a prolonged adult phase during which individuals continue to invest heavily in somatic growth while simultaneously allocating resources to repeated spawning events, a classic iteroparous strategy among tropical mackerels.

The timing of these developmental milestones has been quantified under controlled thermal conditions that mirror the prevailing sea surface temperatures of the species' natural habitat. In a stable environment maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the age at puberty after hatching has been determined to be approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days]. This two-year period of juvenile development is followed by a substantial adult phase extending to a maximum lifespan of approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] under the same thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The five-year maximum longevity, while modest by the standards of some long-lived temperate teleosts, is consistent with the fast-paced life history typical of warm-water scombrids that experience high natural mortality rates. The alignment of these thermal conditions with field observations from the Mozambique Channel reinforces the reliability of these age estimates for wild populations, where water temperatures hover near this value for much of the year.

Reproductive output in Scomberomorus plurilineatus reflects a high-investment, high-frequency strategy typical of its genus. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the breeding season, at approximately 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], this species achieves a maximum reproductive rate that is best described by examining its two components separately. Spawning females produce a substantial number of eggs per event; each individual can release approximately 12,877 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 12,877 eggs per spawning event]. Furthermore, these spawning events occur with remarkable frequency, with gravid individuals observed to participate in about one spawning event per day [F_R_i = about one spawning event per day] during the peak of the reproductive season. This daily spawning frequency, sustained over a protracted breeding period, is a hallmark of tropical scombrids that rely on high fecundity to offset the intense predation pressure faced by pelagic eggs and planktonic larvae.

Comparative life-history analysis places the Kanadi kingfish firmly within the fast-growing, early-maturing guild of tropical scombrids. A recent study comparing growth parameters among Indo-Pacific mackerels confirmed that Scomberomorus plurilineatus reaches a fork length at puberty of 80 centimeters [Lp = 80 centimeters] at approximately 730 days after hatching [tp = approximately 730 days after hatching] when reared at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], which is notably similar to the maturation schedule of its congener Scomberomorus commerson. This pace of development supports an adult phase spanning several years during which females can achieve a body mass of up to 12,500 grams [Wwi = up to 12,500 grams], a size that facilitates the production of the large clutches described earlier. The entire life cycle—from the 0.000065 gram [Wwb = 0.000065 gram] hatchling to the 12,500 gram adult—is a testament to the species' adaptation to a warm, productive marine environment where rapid growth and high fecundity are favored.
